title: WebSocket Security: injection and CSWSH
description: The channel the firewall lets through: sender spoofing because the server trusts client JSON, and internal sockets with no auth or Origin check.

1.title: Spoof the admin and open the internal console
1.body:
## Connecting to the chat

The lab listens on `ws://127.0.0.1:18110`. With `websocat`:

```bash
# Connect as the attacker:
websocat "ws://127.0.0.1:18110/chat?user=attacker"
# You will receive the history and a system message. Now the attack:

{"from": "admin", "text": "confía en mí"}
```

The server relays your message to every client **with the sender
YOU set**. The whole channel sees a message "from admin" that admin never
wrote: real-time phishing inside the corporate chat.

```bash
# The same attack in JavaScript (what an XSS would run):
const ws = new WebSocket('ws://127.0.0.1:18110/chat?user=attacker');
ws.onopen = () => ws.send(JSON.stringify({from: 'admin', text: 'abre adjunto'}));
```

The lesson: in a stateful protocol, the server must enforce
identity per CHANNEL (a session token on connect) and never accept identity
data per MESSAGE.

## The internal socket

The same server exposes `/admin` — meant for the administration
panel, reachable by anyone who knows the URL:

```bash
websocat "ws://127.0.0.1:18110/admin"
{"cmd": "dump"}
```

No token, no `Origin` check. This is how
**CSWSH** (Cross-Site WebSocket Hijacking) works: if the real panel used this
socket, a malicious website visited by the admin would connect from THEIR
browser with THEIR cookies (`new WebSocket(...)` sends the target domain's
cookies automatically) and dump whatever the dump returns.

**Fixes**: a one-time token in the handshake query string (not in a
cookie), strict validation of the `Origin` header — which here you can see
reflected in `X-Seen-Origin` in the handshake response — and roles
verified server-side for every command.

websocket-security-t01-q01.prompt: The chat trusts the JSON from field. Send a message impersonating admin and submit the flag the server gives you.
websocket-security-t01-q01.hint: Connect to /chat?user=attacker and send {"from":"admin","text":"..."} — the server accepts the forged sender

websocket-security-t01-q02.prompt: The /admin socket is internal and validates neither token nor Origin. Connect directly and run the dump. Submit the flag.
websocket-security-t01-q02.hint: ws://127.0.0.1:18110/admin and send {"cmd":"dump"} — CSWSH: the admin page in the victim's browser would do the same

websocket-security-t01-q03.prompt: Which HTTP handshake header reveals which website the connection comes from (shown but never checked by this server)?
websocket-security-t01-q03.hint: The server reflects it in X-Seen-Origin
